seo_title: Xactimate Line Items Missing From Roof Claims (Checklist)
meta_description: Common Xactimate line items missing from roof claims: starter, ridge cap, drip edge, flashing, steep charges and more. See what to check and how to fix it.
h1: Common Xactimate Line Items Missing From Roof Claims
primary_keyword: xactimate line items missing from roof claims
excerpt: Starter, ridge cap, drip edge, flashing, steep charges, debris removal: the Xactimate line items most often missing from roof claims, and how Texas owners recover them.
key_takeaways: Most underpaid roof claims are scope problems: line items never added to the estimate.
Starter, ridge cap, drip edge, flashing, and vents are the most commonly missed items.
Steep and high roof labor charges disappear when pitch or height is misread.
Waste factor and measurement errors shrink quantities even when items are listed.
Request the full estimate, compare line by line, then supplement or consider appraisal.
body_html:
The most common Xactimate line items missing from roof claims are starter shingles, hip and ridge cap, drip edge, ice and water shield, step and counter flashing, pipe jacks, vents, steep and high roof charges, and debris removal. Each omission looks small, but together they can leave a roof claim thousands of dollars short.

Most insurance carriers write roof estimates in Xactimate. The software is precise, but it only prices what the adjuster enters. If a component never makes it onto the estimate, it never makes it into your check.

This guide walks through the Xactimate line items most often left out of roof claims, why they get missed, how Texas codes and conditions factor in, and what you can do when your estimate comes up short.

How Xactimate roof estimates work

Xactimate is estimating software that pairs line items (like "remove laminated shingles" or "R&R drip edge") with regional pricing data for labor and materials. Pricing updates regularly and varies by ZIP code, which is why the same roof can price differently in Amarillo and Austin. For more on pricing, see how Xactimate pricing works in Texas.

The key point is the difference between scope and price. Price is what each line item costs. Scope is which line items are included and in what quantities. Most underpaid roof claims are not a pricing problem. They are a scope problem: items that should be on the estimate simply are not there.

The most common Xactimate line items missing from roof claims

These components appear on nearly every shingle roof replacement but frequently get dropped or under-measured on carrier estimates.

Line itemWhat it isWhy it gets missed
Starter courseFirst row of shingles at eaves and rakesAssumed to be "included" in the shingle line
Hip and ridge capShingles covering hips and ridgesLeft off or measured short
Drip edgeMetal edge at eaves and rakesTreated as reusable or not required
Ice and water shieldSelf-adhered membrane at valleys and penetrationsSwapped for standard felt
Step and counter flashingMetal at walls and chimneysAssumed reusable
Pipe jacks and ventsPenetration boots and ventilationCounted short or skipped
Steep and high roof chargesLabor adders for pitch and heightPitch misread or two-story height ignored
Tear-off, haul, and dumpsterRemoval and disposalPartial layers or disposal left out

Starter shingles

Starter strips run along the eaves and, under most manufacturer instructions, the rakes. They seal the first course and resist wind uplift. Xactimate generally treats starter as a separate line item from field shingles, so if the estimate does not list it, it is not paid. Check that the linear footage matches your eave and rake measurements.

Ridge and hip cap shingles

Hip and ridge cap is priced by the linear foot. Estimates sometimes omit it entirely or use quantities that match only the main ridge, ignoring hips. On a hip roof, that difference is substantial.

Drip edge

Drip edge protects the deck edge and fascia from water. Many Texas cities have adopted versions of the International Residential Code that call for drip edge on shingle roofs, and many manufacturers specify it. Bent or painted-over drip edge rarely survives a tear-off intact, so "reuse" assumptions deserve a second look.

Underlayment and ice and water shield

Felt or synthetic underlayment should cover the full roof area. Ice and water shield, where local code or the manufacturer requires it, typically goes in valleys and around penetrations. Carrier estimates sometimes list only felt, or list underlayment at a smaller quantity than the shingles.

Flashing, pipe boots, and vents frequently missed

Flashing is one of the most overlooked parts of any roof estimate. Step flashing along sidewalls, counter flashing at chimneys, apron flashing, and valley metal are often assumed to be reusable. In reality, step flashing is woven into the shingle courses and is commonly replaced during a full tear-off. Our article on why flashing is commonly missed in claims goes deeper.

Roof penetrations are the other weak spot. Look for:

  • Pipe jacks (lead or neoprene boots) for every plumbing vent
  • Box vents, turbines, ridge vent, or power vents, counted correctly
  • Exhaust caps for kitchen and bath fans
  • Chimney cricket or saddle, where present
  • Skylight flashing kits

Detach and reset items

Satellite dishes, solar panels, antennas, and gutter guards often must come off and go back on. "Detach and reset" line items cover that labor. Solar detach and reset in particular can be a significant cost and is easy to miss if the adjuster did not note the system.

Labor-related line items often excluded

Xactimate adjusts labor for difficult conditions, but only if the adjuster adds the right line items.

  • Steep roof charges: added for pitches commonly at 7/12 and above, with higher tiers for steeper slopes. A misread pitch drops the charge entirely.
  • High roof charges: added when the roof is two stories or higher. They are often missing on two-story homes.
  • Additional layers: removing a second layer of shingles is extra labor and disposal.
  • Access and material handling: tight lots, fences, or landscaping that limit equipment access.
  • Safety setup: roof jacks, harness anchors, and fall protection on steep slopes.

General contractor overhead and profit

When a repair reasonably requires a general contractor to coordinate multiple trades, such as roofing, gutters, siding, and interior drywall, many estimates add overhead and profit (often written as O&P). Carriers frequently leave O&P off roof-only estimates even when other trades are clearly involved. Whether it applies depends on the complexity of the job and your policy, but its absence is worth questioning when three or more trades are needed.

Gutters, fascia, and related exterior items

Gutters, downspouts, and gutter guards often take hail damage alongside the roof, and gutters sometimes must be detached so drip edge can be replaced properly. Look for line items covering gutter detach and reset or replacement, fascia repair, and paint where needed. Like roofing components, these are separate entries and are easy to overlook in a roof-focused inspection.

You can check your own roof's pitch and squares with our roof square, pitch, and waste factor calculator.

Debris removal and cleanup items commonly missing

A roof replacement generates tons of debris. Estimates should account for tear-off, haul-off, dumpster rental or dump fees, and site protection. Look for these line items:

  • Tear-off of each layer, priced per square
  • Haul debris or dumpster load, sized to the job
  • Tarps and protection for landscaping, pools, and siding
  • Magnetic nail sweep of the yard and driveway

Building code and manufacturer requirements

When a roof is replaced, local codes and manufacturer installation instructions dictate how it must be rebuilt. Items commonly affected include drip edge, ice barrier, ventilation balancing, deck re-nailing, and replacing damaged or spaced decking.

Whether these costs are paid depends on your policy. Many Texas homeowners policies include some ordinance or law coverage, while others limit or exclude it. Read ordinance and law coverage explained to understand how code upgrades are handled.

Tip: Ask your local building department or roofer which code edition your city enforces. Codes vary across Texas, and a written code reference is far stronger than "the roofer said so."

Waste factor and quantity errors

Even when the right items are listed, the quantities may be wrong. Shingle quantities should include a waste factor that reflects how cut-up the roof is. A simple gable roof might need a modest waste percentage; a complex hip roof with valleys, dormers, and turrets needs more.

Common measurement problems include:

  1. Using a generic waste percentage regardless of roof complexity
  2. Missing detached garages, porches, or lower roof sections
  3. Measuring eaves and rakes short, which shrinks starter and drip edge
  4. Rounding down squares instead of using actual measured area

See how roof waste factors affect insurance estimates for the details.

Why missing line items matter so much in Texas

Texas sees frequent, severe hail across the Panhandle, North Texas, Central Texas, and the Hill Country. After a big storm in Fort Worth or San Antonio, adjusters may write hundreds of roof estimates in a short time. Under that pressure, small items fall off the estimate.

Roof styles here add complexity, too: steep hip roofs, two-story homes, and laminated shingles that must be matched across slopes. Each of those conditions triggers line items that a rushed estimate can miss. Texas's prompt-payment law (Insurance Code Chapter 542) sets deadlines for handling claims, but it does not guarantee the scope is complete. That part is up to you.

How to identify and recover missing Xactimate items

Follow these steps when your roof estimate looks light:

  1. Get the full estimate. Ask for the complete Xactimate estimate with line items, quantities, and the price list date, not just a summary.
  2. Compare against the roof. Walk through the table above and confirm each item appears with a realistic quantity.
  3. Get an independent estimate. A roofer's estimate or an independent Xactimate estimate written in the same format makes line-by-line comparison easy.
  4. Document and request a supplement. Send photos, measurements, and code references for each missing item. See supplemental insurance claims explained.
  5. Consider appraisal if the gap persists. When the carrier agrees the roof is covered but will not budge on scope or price, appraisal can resolve the amount of loss.
Not sure what your roof estimate is missing? TX Insurance Appraiser reviews carrier Xactimate estimates line by line and can tell you whether the gap justifies a supplement or appraisal. Request a free claim review.

Next steps for an underpaid roof estimate

Missing Xactimate line items are one of the most common reasons Texas roof claims come up short. Starter, ridge cap, drip edge, flashing, vents, labor adders, and debris removal are small individually but add up fast.

Request the full estimate, compare it against your actual roof, and get an independent line-item estimate when the numbers do not match. If the carrier will not correct the scope, appraisal is a policy-based path to a binding amount of loss.

faqs.q: What roof items are most often left off Xactimate estimates?
faqs.a: The items most commonly missing are starter shingles, hip and ridge cap, drip edge, ice and water shield, step and counter flashing, pipe jacks, vents, steep and high roof labor charges, detach and reset items like satellite dishes or solar panels, and debris removal. Each is a separate line item in Xactimate, so if it is not listed, it is not paid.

faqs.q: Is starter shingle included in the shingle line item in Xactimate?
faqs.a: Generally, no. Xactimate typically treats the starter course as its own line item priced by the linear foot along eaves and, per many manufacturer instructions, rakes. If your estimate lists field shingles but no starter, ask the adjuster to add it with a quantity matching your measured eave and rake lengths.

faqs.q: When does a roof qualify for steep roof charges?
faqs.a: Xactimate steep charges commonly begin around a 7/12 pitch, with higher tiers for steeper slopes, because crews work slower and need more safety equipment. If the adjuster misreads the pitch or measures only part of the roof, the charge may be missing. A pitch gauge reading or measurement report helps support the correction.

faqs.q: How do I get missing line items added to my roof claim?
faqs.a: Request the complete line-item estimate, identify each missing component, and send the insurer a written supplement request with photos, measurements, manufacturer instructions, and code references. An independent Xactimate estimate makes comparison easier. If the carrier still refuses and the dispute is about the amount of loss, your policy's appraisal clause may provide a path to resolution.

faqs.q: Are code upgrades like drip edge paid on a Texas roof claim?
faqs.a: It depends on your policy and local code. Many Texas cities enforce versions of the International Residential Code that require drip edge and other components. Whether the insurer pays for upgrades beyond what existed before the loss depends on your ordinance or law coverage, so review your declarations page and endorsements.
